name: Slutsk Belt
description: Woven silk belt produced from the mid-18th century at the Slutsk manufactory of the Radziwiłł family in present-day Belarus, worn with the kontusz coat by Polish-Lithuanian nobility. Double-sided silk with gold and silver thread, floral and checkered borders and maker's marks woven into the ends; genuine Slutsk belts were prized across the Commonwealth and are now a national symbol of Belarus.
maker: Slutsk manufactory, founded by Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł
source: National Museum of Belarus, Slutsk belt collection

name: Romanian Blouse (Ie)
description: Traditional Romanian blouse, the ie, a linen or cotton chemise whose sleeves and shoulders carry dense geometric embroidery; the shoulder ornament, altița, marks the wearer's region and status. Worn in village dress through the 20th century, the ie entered art and fashion through painters such as Matisse; in 2022 UNESCO inscribed 'the traditional blouse with altița'.
material: linen or cotton, cotton or silk thread
source: UNESCO ICH 'The traditional blouse with altița' (2022, Romania)

name: Cimbalom (Hungarian Hammered Dulcimer)
description: Large hammered dulcimer of Hungary, a trapezoid box with rows of metal strings struck by small wooden hammers; the concert cimbalom developed in Budapest in the 1870s. It appears in Romani music and in the works of composers such as Kodály and Bartók, while its village relatives are played across Eastern Europe; the Hungarian word cimbalom names the whole family of hammered dulcimers.
material: wood box, metal strings, wooden hammers
era: concert form from the 1870s; village instruments older
source: Hungarian cimbalom tradition; Kodály and Bartók repertoire

name: Tubeteika (Tatar Skullcap)
description: Hemispherical embroidered skullcap, the traditional headwear of Tatar men. Decorated with silk or velvet embroidery in floral and geometric patterns, the tubeteika was worn at home and in public, while the taller cone-shaped kelepush was worn outdoors. Embroidered tubeteikas were part of festive dress and remain a symbol of Tatar national identity.
source: National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan; tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'

name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)
description: Velvet cap worn by Tatar women, richly embroidered with gold thread, pearls and gilt coins, with a long embroidered tail or tassel hanging down the back. Part of a woman's dowry, the kalfak was the most original piece of Tatar women's festive headwear and demanded great skill in gold embroidery; unlike the man's tubeteika it marked marital status and rank.
material: velvet, gold thread, pearls, gilt coins
source: tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'; National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Kumgan (Tatar Copper Ewer)
description: Narrow-necked copper or brass ewer with a spout and handle used by the Tatars for water and for the ritual ablution before Muslim prayer. Made by Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), the kumgan was a symbol of the Tatar home, kept with a towelled basin and used at festivals and religious observances. Kazan and the villages of Zakazanye produced the finest examples.
maker: Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), Kazan and Zakazanye workshops
source: ar.culture.ru 'Kumgan' (Tatarstan museums); National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan
